summary: Specifies Virtual Enterprise Traversal, a way to automatically provision addresses and prefixes and support internetworking across the varied link types of enterprise networks, including those connected to provider networks or the Internet. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: VET turns a whole enterprise network into what looks like one link. Border routers at the edges wrap packets so that they appear to travel in a single hop, and the document explains how addresses, routes and the discovery of the right exit router are arranged.

questions: how are ip prefixes provisioned across enterprise networks automatically
how does vet present an enterprise as a single ip hop
what is the difference between rlocs and eids
how are enterprise border routers discovered in vet
how does vet register an enterprise prefix
subtitle: A tunnel abstraction that makes a whole enterprise network look like one IP hop.

tldr.problem: Enterprise networks mix link types and hold addresses from several sources, so nodes cannot be configured one at a time by hand and cannot rely on a single routing domain to reach the rest of the enterprise.
tldr.mechanism: VET gives every border router a tunnel interface that encapsulates inner packets in an outer header, so all border routers in the enterprise appear as single-hop neighbours, with separate locator and endpoint addresses and a discovery procedure that finds the right exit for a destination.
tldr.outcome: The document describes address autoconfiguration through DHCPv6 prefix delegation, router discovery and prefix registration, SEAL encapsulation and the mobility, multicast and partitioning cases that follow from the abstraction.

today: RFC 5558 is an Informational Independent Submission published in February 2010, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It carries an IESG note that it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard, and it records that the IETF AUTOCONF Working Group was working on a similar protocol solution at the time.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Enterprise networks connect routers over many kinds of link, and may also connect to provider networks or to the global Internet. The term covers a wide range of cases: a small office or home office network, a mobile ad hoc network whose topology changes over time and which may have little active management, a multi-organizational corporation, or the interdomain core of the Internet itself. The same principles are meant to apply to all of them.

VET is an abstraction for autoconfiguration and internetworking operation in these networks, covering both IPv4 and IPv6. Standard DHCP and neighbor discovery mechanisms are assumed unless stated otherwise. An enterprise router has several kinds of interface: enterprise-interior, enterprise-edge, provider-edge, internal virtual, and VET interfaces used for IP-in-IP encapsulation. Autoconfiguration of provider interfaces is out of scope, because that has to be coordinated with the service provider.

The enterprise must be able to support both provider-independent prefixes and provider-aggregated prefixes, which matters especially when mobility and multihoming are involved. Ingress filtering for multihomed sites, adaptation based on authenticated ICMP feedback from routers on the path, tunnel path MTU mitigation and routing scaling suppression are also in scope.

The document notes that VET is a functional superset of 6over4 and of the Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol, and that it supports further encapsulations such as IPsec and SEAL. It also notes that the IETF AUTOCONF Working Group was working on a similar protocol solution that might become available in the future, and that the publication carried an IESG note saying the RFC is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: An enterprise can be a home network, a corporation, a mobile ad hoc network or the Internet itself. VET is a set of mechanisms that lets nodes in any of these set themselves up and reach each other without hand configuration.

sections.title: EIDs, RLOCs and the Roles of the Routers
sections.content:
The mechanisms build on IP-in-IP encapsulation. The inner IP address, protocol, header and packet are the ones before encapsulation; the outer ones are after it. A mid-layer encapsulation such as IPsec or SEAL may sit between the two layers.

Three router roles are defined. An enterprise router is a fixed or mobile router with a router function, a host function, one or more enterprise-interior interfaces, and possibly internal virtual, enterprise-edge, provider-edge and VET interfaces. An enterprise border router is an enterprise router that connects edge networks to the enterprise or connects several enterprises together; it is a tunnel endpoint and configures a separate VET interface over each set of interfaces belonging to a given enterprise. An enterprise border gateway is a border router that connects VET interfaces over child enterprises to a provider network, either directly or through another VET interface over a parent enterprise.

Two kinds of address are used. A routing locator is a non-link-local address taken from a provider-independent or provider-aggregated prefix that can appear in the enterprise-interior and interdomain routing tables. Enterprise routers use routing locators to run the interior routing protocol and to decide the next hop for packets addressed to other locators, and a VET interface treats them as the outer address when it encapsulates a packet. An endpoint interface identifier is an address taken from a provider-independent or provider-aggregated prefix that is routable within an enterprise-edge or VET overlay scope and may also appear in mapping tables. Edge network routers use these to run the edge routing protocol and to decide the next hop, end systems use them as the addresses they talk to each other on, and a VET interface treats them as the inner address when it encapsulates a packet. The two prefix spaces are typically separate and distinct.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router has two kinds of address. The routing locator says where the router is and is used by the network to route packets. The endpoint identifier says which host is being addressed and is used by the hosts themselves. A tunnel wraps a packet that uses the first kind inside a packet that uses the second.

sections.title: Enterprise Characteristics
sections.content:
An enterprise may be as simple as a few routers with their attached edge networks, and it may contain other enterprises or be part of a larger one. If the link types in an enterprise have similar properties, such as the same Layer 2 address format and the same maximum transmission unit, the enterprise can run a sub-IP layer routing service, and IP then sees the enterprise as an ordinary shared link like a bridged campus network. A single IP hop is then enough to cross the enterprise without IP layer encapsulation. When the link types differ, or the enterprise runs several IP subnets, the enterprise has to provide a routing service that operates at the IP layer, several IP hops may be needed to cross it, and care has to be taken to avoid multi-link subnet problems.

A router in an enterprise embodies both a host function and a router function. The host function supports endpoint-identifier-based and routing-locator-based communication under the weak end-system model. The router function takes part in the enterprise-interior routing protocol, connects the router's edge networks to the enterprise, and may connect the enterprise to provider networks.

Each distinct enterprise needs a trust basis that is established and applied consistently. Where border routers set up symmetric security associations, mechanisms such as IPsec can give authentication and confidentiality. In other scenarios an asymmetric mechanism such as SEcure Neighbor Discovery may be needed, with trust anchors. Enterprises with a centralised management structure can use a name service and a synchronised set of border gateways to support traversal, with the gateways offering a default mapper service for short-term packet forwarding until neighbour relationships between border routers exist. Enterprises with a distributed structure, such as mobile ad hoc networks, may need the border routers to coordinate with each other directly.
sections.plainLanguage: Some enterprises are simple enough that one hop is enough to cross them. Others mix link types and need a routing service of their own. Either way, each enterprise needs an agreed way to decide who belongs to it and how its members trust each other.

sections.title: Autoconfiguration
sections.content:
A router joining an enterprise first configures a unique IPv6 link-local address on each enterprise-interior interface, and an IPv4 link-local address where one is needed. It then configures a routing locator on each of those interfaces and takes part in the routing protocols there. The locator can come from explicit management, from DHCP autoconfiguration, from self-generation out of a large pool, or from another autoconfiguration mechanism. A router can also request prefix delegations over an enterprise-interior interface and assign them on its edge interfaces, and it may obtain a routing locator from a DHCP exchange that uses a temporary self-generated locator as the relay address until the delegated one arrives. Where self-generation is used alone, the router has to keep checking that its locators stay unique.

A border router configures a VET interface over the set of interfaces belonging to one enterprise, initializes it and gives it link-local addresses. When IPv6 is the inner protocol and IPv4 the outer one, it configures an ISATAP link-local address, which embeds an IPv4 routing locator and therefore does not need its own uniqueness check. It then discovers the list of border gateways for each of its VET interfaces, from routing information, from a potential router list discovery mechanism, from DHCP options, or from advertisements on the rasadv multicast group. Even without routing information, the list can be found by resolving an identifying name for the potential router list, formed as a host name and an enterprise-specific DNS suffix. The default host name is isatap, so the name is isatap.example.com when the enterprise's suffix is known; the name assigned to the global Internet interdomain routing core is isatap.net. The name is resolved through an enterprise-local name service in centrally managed enterprises, or through Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution over the VET interface in distributed ones, where every border gateway answers and the router accepts the union of the replies.

After discovery the border router configures endpoint identifiers. It can obtain provider-aggregated prefixes from the border gateways through a DHCP exchange in which the gateways act as relays or servers, using automated IPv4 prefix delegation or DHCPv6 prefix delegation over the VET interface, with either a two-message or a four-message exchange. The router can propose a specific prefix, and the server checks it for consistency and uniqueness before returning it. After receiving provider-aggregated prefixes it can provision them on its edge interfaces and on other VET interfaces where it is itself a gateway.

Provider-independent prefixes can also be acquired, self-configured or delegated by a registration authority, and when it does so the router must also obtain credentials that let it prove ownership of the prefix when it registers it with the border gateways. The minimum IPv6 provider-independent prefix a border router may acquire is a /56, and the minimum IPv4 one is a /24. A border gateway configures its provider-edge interfaces in the way the provider requires, adds one or more of its locators for the child enterprise to the potential router list, and keeps those resource records up to date. To avoid loops it must not configure a default route on a VET interface over a child enterprise.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers pick up their addresses by themselves: a locator from DHCP or by generating one, and endpoint identifiers from the border gateways through a prefix delegation exchange. To find the border gateways, a router resolves a name that the enterprise has agreed on.

sections.title: Internetworking Operation
sections.content:
Router discovery in an enterprise follows the ISATAP procedures. Border gateways send solicited router advertisements over their VET interfaces, carrying prefix information options with provider-aggregated prefixes for stateless address autoconfiguration. Nodes in the enterprise discover the gateways, then send unicast router solicitations over their VET interfaces to receive advertisements, and may need to use SEcure Neighbor Discovery to secure the exchange depending on the enterprise's trust basis. On receiving an advertisement the node authenticates it, configures a default route from the router lifetime, and configures addresses from the advertised prefixes when the relevant options are present. Where DHCPv6 is preferred, the DHCP exchange between border routers and gateways may carry the default router and prefix information instead, and the solicitation exchange may not be needed.

Provider-aggregated prefixes stay active at the gateways as long as the border router keeps renewing its DHCP lease, and the lease also keeps the state alive through a temporary partition of the network. Provider-independent prefixes are registered differently: the border router sends router advertisements carrying route information options with its provider-independent prefixes to one or more border gateways, using an outer locator as the destination and a link-local address on the VET interface as the inner destination. A gateway authenticates the advertisement, discards it if authentication fails, and otherwise installs the prefixes in its forwarding table, configured both for ingress filtering and for forwarding. It then publishes each /56 provider-independent prefix as a separate fully qualified domain name made of fourteen nibbles in reverse order followed by the string ip6 and the potential router list name, and includes the outer locator of the advertisement in the publication. The gateway then acts as a neighbour discovery proxy on the VET interfaces of its parent enterprises and relays the advertisement onwards, recursively, until a border router attached to an interdomain routing core is reached. The owner of the prefixes must send further advertisements periodically to refresh the lifetimes. A similar procedure, with an ICMPv6 redirect carrying link-layer address options, lets a node find the right exit for a destination prefix, by querying the name service for the /56 prefix in the destination address, or by sending the first packet to a default route and letting the gateway redirect it. In enterprises where spoofing is possible, a router must send authenticating credentials before it forwards packets through a newly discovered next hop.

Forwarding over a VET interface consults the forwarding table to pick the next-hop border router or gateway, using default router preferences, routing protocol information or traffic engineering configuration when several are available. The interface encapsulates the inner packet in any mid-layer headers followed by an outer header and hands it to the outer forwarding engine. VET interfaces are advised to use SEAL encapsulation, which keeps a per-packet identifier, the SEAL_ID, that increases by one for each packet. That identifier lets a receiver confirm that an error message refers to a packet it really sent, lets a gateway drop packets with identifiers outside the current window, and gives a way to ask a next hop to confirm that it is reachable.

Errors are handled with the usual ICMP messages. A border router that has no ingress filter entry for a received packet drops it and returns a destination unreachable message saying the source address failed the ingress and egress policy, subject to rate limiting. One that has no forwarding entry for the destination returns a destination unreachable message saying there is no route. On receiving a policy failure message, the router suspends forwarding through the locator that sent it and lets other locators for the same prefix carry the traffic, and it deletes the entry altogether if too many errors arrive. Multicast is mapped from the inner multicast address space onto a site-scoped outer multicast address space, and service discovery can be done with Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution over the VET interface or with multicast DNS over an underlying interface. An enterprise can be partitioned physically, by running a separate VET interface over each set of underlying interfaces with its own potential router list name, or logically, by sending advertisements that carry different prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside an enterprise, a node finds its way out by listening for advertisements from the border gateways and, when it has a packet for a distant destination, by asking the name service or by trying a default route and accepting a redirect. Packets are then wrapped in an outer header and sent through the enterprise as if it were one link.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security considerations for mobile ad hoc networks are given in RFC 2501, and the security considerations for tunnelling that apply to VET are found in RFC 2529 and RFC 5214. In particular, a VET node must verify that the outer IP source address of a packet received on a VET interface is correct for the inner IP source address, using the procedures of Section 7.3 of RFC 5214 together with the ingress filtering mechanisms described in the document.

SEcure Neighbor Discovery, IPsec and SEAL provide additional protection against spoofed source addresses and bogus router advertisements sent by rogue routers. Rogue routers can send advertisements with spoofed locator addresses, consuming network resources and causing gateways to do extra work, but the memo advises that gateways should not blacklist those locators, because that would deny service to their legitimate owners.
sections.plainLanguage: The outer address of a received packet has to match the inner one, or the packet is dropped. Rogue routers are not banned outright, because banning an address would also cut off the real owner of that address.

Routers, for the interior routing protocol and next-hop selection
Hosts and edge routers, as the address of the endpoint

viz.caption: WHAT THE VET INTERFACE DOES FOR A NODE

items.title: Encapsulation
items.text: The inner packet is wrapped in any mid-layer headers and an outer IP header before it leaves the enterprise.

items.title: Single-hop appearance
items.text: All border routers in the enterprise look like neighbours on one virtual link.

items.title: Next-hop discovery
items.text: A name lookup or an ICMP redirect tells the node which border router to use for a destination prefix.

items.title: SEAL identifiers
items.text: A per-packet counter lets a receiver confirm that an error message refers to a packet it sent.
